topics.title: HIPAA, Privacy & Confidentiality
topics.exemplar: 49.C Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act

topics.title: Mandatory Reporting: What Nurses Must Report

flashcards.front: What does HIPAA stand for, and when was it passed?
flashcards.back: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, a 1996 federal law.

flashcards.front: List the four things HIPAA does (per your slides).
flashcards.back: 1) Reduces barriers related to preexisting conditions. 2) Protects people who lose prior coverage. 3) Eliminates medical underwriting for group insurance plans. 4) Protects patient health information (Privacy Rule).

flashcards.front: What is a preexisting condition, and what does current law add to HIPAA?
flashcards.back: A health problem you had before new coverage began. HIPAA limited exclusions; since 2014 the Affordable Care Act bars most plans from excluding them.

flashcards.front: What does “eliminates medical underwriting for group plans” mean?
flashcards.back: A group plan (like a work plan) cannot turn away one member or charge them more because of their health history.

flashcards.front: Define protected health information (PHI).
flashcards.back: Any identifiable information about a client’s past, present, or future physical or mental health, the care provided, or payment for care. Spoken, paper, or electronic.

flashcards.front: A post leaves out the client’s name but gives age, crash location, and date. Is it PHI?
flashcards.back: Yes. Those details can identify the client. Only fully de-identified data is not PHI. Never post about clients.

flashcards.front: Privacy vs. confidentiality?
flashcards.back: Privacy: the client’s right to control what personal information is shared. Confidentiality: the nurse’s obligation to protect that information once it has been disclosed.

flashcards.front: Name the three actions confidentiality applies to.
flashcards.back: Obtaining (access only what you need for care), disclosing (share only with those directly involved in care), and advocating (always protect client privacy).

flashcards.front: With whom may PHI be shared without written authorization (per your slide)?
flashcards.back: The client, health care providers involved in care, and insurance/payers for billing and authorization. Reports required by law are also allowed.

flashcards.front: What is the HIPAA Privacy Rule?
flashcards.back: National standards for how PHI in any form may be used and shared, plus client rights such as seeing and copying their record.

flashcards.front: What is the HIPAA Security Rule?
flashcards.back: Rules protecting electronic PHI with administrative (training, access policies), physical (locked areas, screen placement), and technical (unique logins, auto logoff, encryption, audit logs) safeguards.

flashcards.front: What is the minimum necessary standard, and what is its big exception?
flashcards.back: Use, request, or share only the least PHI needed. It does not limit provider-to-provider sharing for treatment or what the client may see.

flashcards.front: A nurse opens a neighbor’s chart but tells no one. Breach?
flashcards.back: Yes. Accessing PHI with no work reason is a breach. Audit logs record every chart opened.

flashcards.front: You fax PHI to the wrong number. What do you do?
flashcards.back: Stop it if you can (call, ask them to destroy it), report right away to your supervisor or privacy officer, and complete an incident report. Never cover it up.

flashcards.front: Name three social media rules for nurses.
flashcards.back: No client photos or posts (even without names); no PHI in personal texts; don’t friend current clients. Privacy settings don’t make posts private, and deleting doesn’t erase them.

flashcards.front: Who enforces HIPAA, and who else can act on a privacy breach by a nurse?
flashcards.back: The HHS Office for Civil Rights enforces HIPAA. The employer may fire, the Board of Nursing may discipline (in NC, the NCBON), and the client may sue under state law.

flashcards.front: Define mandatory reporting.
flashcards.back: A legal requirement for health care professionals to report certain acts, events, or conditions to a designated agency.

flashcards.front: What reporting path does your slide show?
flashcards.back: The facility’s administrative chain: charge nurse → supervisor → designated reporting body. But the report must actually reach the agency; telling a supervisor is not always enough.

flashcards.front: What is good faith immunity?
flashcards.back: Legal protection for nurses who report suspected abuse or violations honestly. It applies even if the abuse is not confirmed.

flashcards.front: Is disclosing PHI to report abuse a HIPAA violation?
flashcards.back: No. HIPAA allows disclosures required by law. Share only what the report needs.

flashcards.front: Whose abuse or neglect must nurses report (slide 27)?
flashcards.back: Children; older adults and dependent adults; vulnerable or disabled individuals. Laws vary by state, so follow facility policy.

flashcards.front: Which specific injuries and illnesses are on your slide’s reporting list?
flashcards.back: Gunshot wounds, stab wounds, injuries from criminal acts or violence, poisonings, and certain infectious diseases (per public health rules). Exact rules vary by state.

flashcards.front: Where do reports of impaired, unsafe, or unethical nursing practice go?
flashcards.back: To the Board of Nursing (Nurse Practice Act violations), through facility policy. In NC, the NCBON, which offers alternative-to-discipline programs for substance use.

flashcards.front: Do you need proof before reporting suspected child abuse?
flashcards.back: No. Report reasonable suspicion promptly. Do not investigate, confront, or wait for test results.

flashcards.front: NC: who must report suspected child maltreatment, and to whom?
flashcards.back: Any person or institution (universal reporting, G.S. 7B-301) reports to the county DSS director. Knowingly failing to report is a crime.

flashcards.front: NC: where are suspected abuse or neglect of disabled adults reported?
flashcards.back: To the county DSS director, orally or in writing (G.S. 108A-102). Good-faith reporters are immune.

flashcards.front: Where are reportable communicable diseases reported? Give examples.
flashcards.back: To the local (in NC) or state health department. Examples: TB, measles, pertussis, syphilis, gonorrhea, chlamydia, HIV, hepatitis.

flashcards.front: How do you protect evidence from a gunshot wound victim?
flashcards.back: Treat first. Cut around bullet holes, put each clothing item in its own paper bag, label it, and keep a chain of custody record.

flashcards.front: Signs a nurse may be diverting drugs?
flashcards.back: Signs out more opioids than peers, frequent unwitnessed wastes, clients’ pain unrelieved on that nurse’s shift, wrong counts, frequent breaks or absences.

flashcards.front: A competent adult discloses partner abuse but does not want it reported. What does the nurse do?
flashcards.back: In most states, respect the choice unless a specific law requires a report (such as a gunshot wound). Offer privacy, safety planning, and resources; document.

flashcards.front: A teen asks you to promise not to tell about abuse. Best response?
flashcards.back: Be honest: you can’t keep it secret because you must report it to keep them safe. Never promise total secrecy.
